source.title: Domain-Aware Scaling Laws Uncover Data Synergy
source.authors: K. Hamidieh; L. Mackey; David Alvarez-Melis

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through the appendices, but some extracted figures and table layouts are garbled or flattened.
record.tranche_reason: The study refines domain-agnostic scaling laws with evidence that data composition changes fitted scaling slopes and improves held-out prediction. It also tests whether observational synergy estimates predict mixture rankings.
record.gate_note: The paper tests scaling-law prediction on downstream benchmark pseudo-losses and bits-per-byte, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy. It does not test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, architecture-shape effects, or other modalities and training regimes. The controlled mixture-training results test predicted mixture rankings, not the original large-run loss extrapolation claim.
record.test_reason: The study fits Chinchilla-form laws to downstream benchmark pseudo-losses across 52 open models. It reports how well the domain-agnostic form predicts held-out models (V6), and it argues, using fitted slopes, that the data exponent depends on the pretraining mixture and that α and β are poorly identified (V7). Its mixture-optimisation runs validate the study's own synergy coefficients at fixed scale, not a scaling claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that modelling first-order domain→benchmark and second-order domain-domain synergy improves held-out fit over domain-agnostic scaling laws, gives stable sparse synergy estimates, and correctly predicts optimal versus anti-optimal mixture rankings at 30M and 150M. They caution that the estimates are observational associations, rely on noisy metadata and a low-dimensional mixture space, and are validated only at small scale.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than the original controlled scaling sweeps over model size, data, and compute, this study fits domain-aware laws to observational open-weight model and mixture data, using downstream benchmark pseudo-losses. It adds first- and second-order composition terms and validates predicted mixture rankings with new 30M and 150M runs.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted data exponent and benchmark loss vary with the training mixture. The paper also reports that α and β trade off under correlated model size and token count, while composition coefficients are more stable across folds and seeds.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed scale, mixtures predicted optimal reach lower target-task BPB than mixtures predicted anti-optimal at 30M and 150M parameters. The predicted-optimal mixture is not always better than balanced.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Domain-composition terms fitted observationally predict mixture rankings on downstream task loss.

record.problems: The main scaling-law fit is observational, uses potentially noisy or incomplete mixture metadata, and spans an effectively low-dimensional mixture space. The authors say α and β are not individually well identified, and the controlled validation runs are only 30M and 150M parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant numerical results were omitted. Several figure-only coefficient and residual plots are not separately cataloged where the text does not supply assignable exact values.

untested.parts: No row on held-out pretraining cross-entropy. WikiText and C4 are among the fitted benchmarks, but their baseline R2 values sit in a garbled figure and are rank-transformed.
No extrapolation from small to much larger runs. The cross-validation is over existing models.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
Text pretraining only. No other modalities, repeated-data regimes or fine-tuning.
Predicting task scores from pretraining loss; extrapolating downstream performance to larger scale.
Compute-optimal split; parameter counting; training schedule; systematic comparison of published laws.

missing.what: Chinchilla baseline fitted to HumanEval pass@1 gives R2 −0.11, against 0.41 with BPB. The choice of metric decides whether a scaling fit exists at all.
Tasks where the Chinchilla baseline has negative R2 are excluded, because not all benchmarks show scaling-law behaviour. Which tasks were excluded is not stated.
Per-mixture HumanEval exponents beyond R3 and R4 (no-flan, dolma1.6+, no-reddit, no-math-code). The figure is garbled; values appear to be about 0.40, 0.37, 0.25 and 0.21.
Per-benchmark held-out R2 of the Chinchilla baseline, including the WikiText and C4 language-modelling losses. The figure values are garbled.

record.verdict_notes: The targets are rank-Gaussian-transformed pseudo-losses: task BPB or accuracy, with perplexity for WikiText and C4. None is raw pretraining loss, so V1 to V3 are not tested. R16–R27 validate the study's own method at fixed scale and were unlinked from V6. The V7 evidence concerns the data exponent of downstream-task loss and the α/β identifiability of observational fits, not the compute-optimal split.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits losses or pseudo-losses on downstream benchmarks, not held-out pretraining cross-entropy.
Five-fold held-out prediction across existing models and mixture-ranking validation do not test extrapolating a loss fit from small runs to runs orders of magnitude larger.
No fixed-compute sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token allocation is tested.
The study does not compare architecture depth, width, or other shape choices at fixed parameter count.
The analysis concerns text pretraining; modality and fine-tuning or transfer generality are not tested.

The study predicts downstream benchmark pseudo-losses and reports their association with task scores, but does not establish that score improvements are guaranteed or directly predict score from pretraining loss alone.
The study reports mixture-dependent slopes and fitting identifiability issues, but does not test compute-optimal allocation exponents or systematically compare the original papers' fitting choices.

relationships.condition: Domain-agnostic N,D law on code-benchmark pseudo-losses
relationships.reason: The Chinchilla form explains little held-out variance on code benchmarks: R2 0.41 on HumanEval and 0.20 on MBPP (R5, R7). Per the text, HumanEval pass@1 gives R2 −0.11, and tasks with negative R2 were excluded.
relationships.display_finding: Chinchilla fits achieved held-out R² of 0.41 on HumanEval pseudo-loss and 0.20 on MBPP pseudo-loss, but −0.11 on HumanEval pass@1, with negative-R² tasks excluded.

relationships.condition: Held-out pseudo-loss prediction once mixture-composition terms are added
relationships.reason: Held-out R2 rises to 0.92 (HumanEval) and 0.88 (MBPP), with a median of 0.906 to 0.912 across 11 benchmarks (R6, R8–R10). This is predictability conditional on composition.
relationships.display_finding: Adding mixture-composition terms yielded held-out R² of 0.92 on HumanEval and 0.88 on MBPP, with median R² increasing from 0.906 to 0.912 across 11 benchmarks.

tranche.reason: The study shows limitations of domain-agnostic downstream scaling and demonstrates mixture-dependent exponents and fitting non-identifiability.

reader_labels.reason: The domain-aware fits predict benchmark pseudo-loss on held-out models, with HumanEval and MBPP R2 improving from 0.41 to 0.92 and from 0.20 to 0.88; the aggregate median cross-validated R2 is 0.906 for the first-order model and 0.912 for the second-order model (R5–R10).
